title: Hopfield networks
question: Do Amari's 1972 model and Hopfield's 1982 additions support Schmidhuber's claim that the basic network should be credited to Amari?

usual_credit.summary: The Hopfield network, a recurrent network of binary threshold units with symmetric weights whose dynamics settle into stored patterns, is credited to John Hopfield's 1982 paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Hopfield shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics with Geoffrey Hinton, the committee's scientific background describes the 1982 paper as a dynamical model for an associative memory based on a simple recurrent neural network, and Hinton's Nobel lecture says Hopfield made the weights symmetric so that networks settle to a stable state.

works.title: Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities

claim.summary: Schmidhuber says that Shun'ichi Amari made the Lenz-Ising recurrent architecture adaptive in 1972, so that it could learn to associate input patterns with output patterns through weights that are correlations of the stored patterns, and that Hopfield republished the same basic equations in 1982 without citing that paper. He points out that Hopfield did cite two later Amari papers on self-organisation, that Kaoru Nakano (1972) and William Little (1974) had related models, and that Hopfield's own additions were an analysis of storage capacity and a Lyapunov function for sequential updates. He also says that Hopfield's 1984 analog version did not cite Cohen and Grossberg (1983).

response.summary: Amari's 2024 congratulatory statement credits Hopfield's associative-memory work and capacity simulations. In a 2025 interview, he also says that an identical model had appeared in Japan and that Hopfield cited a later self-organization paper rather than his 1972 associative-memory paper. The Nobel Committee's background document acknowledges Amari, Nakano and Little as earlier contributors and explains the energy-based dynamics of Hopfield's model. These sources recognize both predecessors and later development, but do not contain a direct answer by Hopfield to Schmidhuber's allegation. The distinction at issue includes update rules, convergence analysis and capacity, not just the network diagram.

agreed_facts: Amari published 'Learning patterns and pattern sequences by self-organizing nets of threshold elements' in IEEE Transactions on Computers in 1972, and Hopfield published his paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in April 1982.
Hopfield's 1982 reference list includes two Amari papers on self-organisation, from 1977 and 1978, and not the 1972 paper, a point that Amari himself makes.
The 2024 Nobel committee's scientific background cites Nakano (1972), Amari (1972) and Little (1974) as earlier work on recurrent network models inspired by magnetic systems.
Schmidhuber's report credits Hopfield with an analysis of storage capacity and with a Lyapunov function for sequential neuron updates, in place of Amari's parallel updates.
crux: The dispute is whether Amari's 1972 network and Hopfield's 1982 network are essentially the same model, differing mainly in parallel versus sequential updates, or whether Hopfield's energy function and capacity analysis make the 1982 paper an independent contribution. It also asks whether Hopfield, who cited two other Amari papers, owed a citation to the 1972 paper.
